items.excerpt: Alphabet shares suffer worst-ever single-day fall, USD 500 billion wiped off market value amid AI spending concerns Shares of Google's parent, Alphabet, plunged more than 12 per cent on Thursday, marking their worst single-day decline on record and wiping out around USD 500 billion in market value, as investors grew increasingly concerned about rising artificial intelligence spending and slowing growth in its search advertising business, according to a report by CNN. The decline was larger than any single-day fall recorded during the COVID-19 pandemic or the 2008 financial crisis, the report said. It also marked the second-largest single-day loss in market value in history, after chipmaker Nvidia's nearly USD 600 billion decline in early 2025. The sell-off followed Alphabet's quarterly results, which reported sales below analysts' expectations. Investors were particularly concerned about the outlook for Google's search advertising business, which faces growing competition from AI-powered chatbots that could change how consumers access information online. The report said investors were worried that the shift towards AI-based search could happen faster than Google can respond and adapt its business. At the same time, Alphabet's growing expenditure on AI infrastructure has raised questions about how quickly the company can generate returns from its investments. The company reported USD 51.4 billion in capital expenditure in the third quarter alone, compared with USD 91.4 billion for the entire year in 2025. Its spending includes investments in data centres and other infrastructure required to support AI development. CNN reported that ... This is particularly significant as the company had not reported a negative figure in any quarter since going public in 2004, before becoming Alphabet in 2015.

items.excerpt: Author: Associated Press Published: 12:00 AM EDT October 30, 2026 Updated: 12:04 AM EDT October 30, 2026 Trump cancels rallies in Kansas and Iowa, opting for telerallies to reach more voters, RNC says ROCK HILL, S.C. (AP) — President Donald Trump on Thursday canceled weekend rallies in Iowa and Kansas, opting instead to support Republican candidates with telerallies that his party said could reach more voters in nearly two dozen states in the final days of a midterm election that could cost the GOP control of Congress. The president traveled to South Carolina Thursday for the second time in a month, a sign of Republican anxiety about Darline Graham's ability to fend off a robust challenge from Democrat Annie Andrews for a critical U.S. Senate seat. Voters in South Carolina have not sent a Democrat to the Senate in nearly three decades. But Andrews, a pediatrician who previously ran unsuccessfully for Congress, is urging voters seeking change to “try something new for once.” That message could resonate in an election year defined by voter frustration with the economy, gas prices and the war in Iran, putting Trump's Republican Party on defense in territory where they have rarely had to compete in recent years. Beyond South Carolina, Republicans are entering the final days of this year's midterm elections navigating tight contests in Texas, Kansas, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska. Both parties are also closely following developments in the Mississippi Senate race. Netanyahu’s party claims election 'stolen' as results show him losing majority JERUSALEM (AP) — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's party on Thursday amplified unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, potentially with foreign assistance, as final results showed his bloc had lost its majority in parliament. The opposition accused Netanyahu of demonizing the Arab population after a historic showing by Arab-led parties in an attempt to delegitimize the election. If the rest of the opposition teams up with Arab parties, a rare and politically risky move, they could potentially form a majority government in parliament, the Knesset. Results released by election officials on Thursday showed Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats in the 120-member assembly, well below the 68 seats it had controlled at its peak in the previous parliament. His main opposition won 48 seats and Arab-led parties secured the other 19. The count is complete, but the results still need to be certified and submitted to the country's president next Wednesday. Netanyahu's party, Likud, has been spreading claims of malfeasance by Arab-led parties since exit polls indicated the prime minister had suffered a setback in Tuesday's vote. But it ramped up the rhetoric after the head of Israel's election committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, said that “serious suspicions” of foreign interference had been brought before him. ... Strong growth and inflation paints mixed picture of economy days before midterm elections WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. economic growth was notably strong from July to September, yet inflation accelerated at the same time, new data showed Thursday, painting a mixed picture about the country's economy less than a week before midterm elections in which the uncomfortably high cost of living looms larger than perhaps any other issue. Strong consumer spending and soaring investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure were key drivers of growth in the third quarter. When unemployment is as low as it is right now, consumers often spend at a healthy clip and they are doing so, particularly wealthier Americans who are riding a wave of record stock market gains. The economy grew at a strong 3.4% annual rate in the July-September quarter, the Commerce Department said Thursday, much faster than the 2.2% growth in the April-June quarter. Consumer spending climbed 3.8% at an annual rate, marking the second straight quarter of strong growth and far exceeding the 0.7% increase in the first three months of the year. Business investment, driven by spending on AI infrastructure, jumped 12.7%, the most in six years. Yet economists worry that persistently high prices are eroding Americans' ability to keep up. Thursday's data suggest consumers are increasingly dipping into savings to cover their costs. After-tax incomes, adjusted for inflation, slipped from August to September and were up just 1% from a year earlier. At the same time, inflation-adjusted spending rose 2.5% from a year earlier.

items.title: PCE inflation report September 2026:
items.excerpt: Published Thu, Oct 29 2026 8:32 AM EDT Updated Thu, Oct 29 2026 2:06 PM EDT ... economy grew at a 3.4% pace in the third quarter, faster than expected. - Inflation continued to run above the Fed's 2% target in September, with a headline rate of 3.6% and core at 3.1%, according to the central bank's preferred gauge. ... The pace of price increases stepped up in September, keeping inflation well above the Federal Reserve's target, while the economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter, according to Commerce Department reports Thursday. The personal consumption expenditures price index increased a seasonally adjusted 0.5% for the month, putting the annual inflation rate at 3.6%. The monthly increase was the largest since March but in line with the Dow Jones consensus, while the annual rate was 0.1 percentage point below. Excluding food and energy, the core PCE posted respective readings of 0.3% and 3.1%, in line with the consensus. While the Fed follows both measures closely, officials generally see the core reading as more indicative of longer-term inflation trends. While inflation continued to run ahead of the Fed's 2% target, the Commerce Department also reported that gross domestic product was strong in the third quarter. GDP increased at a seasonally adjusted annualized pace of 3.4%, better than the 3.1% estimate and well ahead of the 2.2% in the second quarter. Also, in September consumer spending proved resilient, climbing 0.5%, a bit below the forecast for a 0.6% gain, while personal income rose 0.2%, compared with the estimate for 0.3%. The reports come the day after the Fed voted to hold its benchmark interest rate in a range between 3.75%-4%. Despite elevated inflation readings, central bank officials insist they can afford to evaluate incoming data before deciding on their next move. "The period right in front of us is information rich. There is a lot that's happening in the world. My colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said Wednesday. However, the data deluge from Thursday shows the Fed could have more work to do. ... Initial jobless claims edged lower to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ended Oct. ... Consumer spending rose 3.8% in the third quarter, the same pace as the prior period. Gross private domestic investment soared 19.4%, driven by a 20.9% surge in equipment spending and an 8.4% jump on intellectual property products. Real sales to private domestic purchasers, a proxy that Fed officials use for underlying demand, rose 4.9%, compared with a 4.6% increase in the second quarter. There was some good inflation news for the period: On a quarterly basis, PCE prices rose 2.1% on the headline number and 2.5% for core, down respectively from 5% and 3.3% in the second quarter. September's price increases were driven largely by a surge in energy costs that economists fear could be spreading to other parts of the economy. Gasoline and other energy goods saw a 9.2% rise for the month while energy goods and services broadly jumped 5.4%. At the same time, services prices excluding energy and housing rose 0.4%, and housing costs increased 0.3%.

items.title: US midterms briefing: Trump spruiks economy as farmer-funded ads attack cost-of-living record - ABC News
items.excerpt: ## Here's what you need to know today - GDP vs inflation: The last economy snapshot before the midterms is out. GDP in the third quarter rose 3.4 per cent annually. "The country is doing unbelievably well," Trump told reporters while en route to a rally in South Carolina. But that message might not cut through to Americans feeling the pinch after inflation sped up in September, with prices surging 3.6 per cent annually (the central bank's target is 2 per cent). The cost of living remains the top issue for voters going into the election. - The tale of two Dans: Alaska's US Senate race involving two Dan Sullivans took another twist yesterday, when the New York Times reported Democrats sought a spoiler candidate by the same name to run against the Republican senator. House Republicans now say they will investigate Mary Peltola, the Democratic challenger who is currently leading in the polls. House Oversight Committee chair James Comer has announced an investigation into the matter and requested interviews with Peltola's former campaign manager and her former chief of staff. But legal experts say unless he concealed financial support, the challenging Sullivan likely didn't break any laws, and political parties are allowed to mislead the public. See my chat with North America correspondent Lauren Day below for another thread in this saga! - Attack ads: This midterm election cycle is the most expensive in history. Where does all that money go? Ads, mostly. And new ones are rolling out every day. A group of farmers is helping to fund $US3 million ($4.2 million) in attack ads against Republicans in some of the country's most competitive races. Trump is already facing headwinds among typically loyal rural supporters due to tariffs and high fuel costs. Meanwhile, in Texas, Elon Musk is funding an AI-powered robocall campaign that (rather ironically) attacks Democratic US Senate candidate James Talarico for allegedly taking money from "data center special interest" groups, CNN reports.

items.title: Trump administration renews bid to block Alaska election results | US Midterm Elections 2026 News | Al Jazeera
items.excerpt: Published On 30 Oct 2026 30 Oct 2026 The United States Department of Justice has filed a revised lawsuit seeking to decertify the results of a Senate race in the state of Alaska if Republican incumbent Dan S Sullivan loses narrowly. The updated lawsuit on Thursday comes just days before the November 3 midterm election, which will determine control of Congress. The complaint accuses Democrats of trying to confuse voters by placing a candidate with the same name as Sullivan on the ballot. Alaska’s Senate race is one of seven key toss-ups that will likely decide whether Republicans keep their majority in Congress’s upper chamber. Democratic challenger Mary Peltola is seeking to unseat Sullivan, a Republican ally of US President Donald Trump. But a New York Times report on Wednesday alleged that members of Peltola’s campaign helped recruit a retired teacher, Dan J Sullivan Jr, to run for the Senate seat as a spoiler candidate, designed to draw votes away from the incumbent. The Times report prompted a renewed legal push under the Trump administration to bar Alaska from certifying its election results, should Senator Sullivan lose. The Department of Justice issued 40 subpoenas and document preservation requests as part of the revised complaint, the Reuters news agency reported. Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy also ordered a criminal investigation into the allegations. Peltola’s campaign has denied involvement in Dan J Sullivan Jr’s bid for the Senate. Prosecutors, however, have accused the Democrat and her allies of playing partisan tricks – and undermining voters as a result. “They orchestrated his sham campaign for the purpose of misleading Alaskan voters and getting Peltola elected,” Justice Department lawyers wrote in their amended complaint. But the Justice Department’s lawsuit has raised concerns about election integrity and federal meddling. Under the US Constitution, election administration falls to the states, not the presidency. In June, Alaska’s Supreme Court ruled that Dan J Sullivan Jr could compete in the midterms, and the state’s election office has already taken steps to reduce confusion between the two Sullivans. Recruiting candidates to split an opponent’s vote – a practice known as ballot stacking – is also generally considered to be legal and has been used by both parties in Alaska. Critics have been sceptical of the Justice Department’s bid to pause the certification of Alaska’s Senate results if Senator Sullivan does not win re-election, noting it would be impossible to divine voter intent based on the final tally alone. Justin Levitt, a former Department of Justice official under President Joe Biden, also questioned what legal authority the federal government had to get involved in the case. “I don’t know what they’re putting out subpoenas to investigate because I don’t know what federal violations are implicated that DOJ would have jurisdiction over,” Levitt told the Associated Press news agency. “Sure makes it seem like the point of the investigation is to become the story.”

items.title: New Music Friday: JISOO, Gracie Abrams, and More!
items.excerpt: InMusic October 29, 2026 New Music Friday arrives on October 30 with fresh releases from JISOO, Gracie Abrams, and more artists closing out the month just ahead of Halloween. JISOO leads the new-release lineup with “ ADDICTED,” her latest solo single as the BLACKPINK member continues building toward her upcoming debut solo studio album. The track arrives less than two months after “ CLICK,” released on September 4, and follows a steady run of solo projects that has included her AMORTAGE EP and “Earthquake” in February 2025, as well as her collaboration with Zayn, “ Eyes Closed,” in October of the same year. Announced by her agency, BLISSOO, on October 24, “ADDICTED” arrives with a striking purple visual identity. The darker aesthetic marks a shift from the colorful carnival imagery associated with “CLICK,” whose music video, directed by Joseph Kahn, placed JISOO in an abandoned amusement park populated by mechanical attractions and animatronic figures. That release reached No. 3 on the worldwide iTunes chart, topped rankings in nine regions and accumulated more than 55 million YouTube views for its music video. Gracie Abrams also has new music for listeners with “ Here You Come, There You Go,” the lead single from the deluxe edition of Daughter from Hell. Scheduled for November 20, the expanded album adds five songs to the original release, bringing its tracklist to 21. The additional tracks are “Here You Come, There You Go,” “Lost In It,” “Crazy Girl,” “Love Letter” and “Out of Nowhere.” The announcement extends the momentum of Abrams’ third studio album, which debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 in July with 124,000 equivalent album units earned in the United States. The achievement marked her first chart-topping album in the country and followed the success of Good Riddance and The Secret of Us. Produced and written alongside longtime collaborator Aaron Dessner, Daughter from Hell explores the uncertainty and emotional turbulence of growing up. Gracie Abrams’ new single also arrives just ahead of her return to Saturday Night Live on October 31, when she will serve as musical guest for the show’s Halloween episode hosted by Inde Navarrette. Noteworthy releases also come from Daddy Yankee, Megan Thee Stallion, Prince, Snoh Aalegra, Dominic Fike, Nickelback, Mariah Carey, and more. Check out the latest music releases this Friday. ## Songs - ADDICTED – JISOO - Here You Come, There You Go – Gracie Abrams - Cosita – Daddy Yankee ft.
